summary: This document updates the IANA registries for MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping defined in RFC 8029 and RFC 8611. For the TLV and sub-TLV registries, the registration procedure formerly called Private Use is changed to First Come First Served. It also clarifies how responses are sent when an unknown or erroneous code point is seen, and aligns the wording with RFC 8126.

eli5.summary: A club keeps a list of codes people can claim. This document changes the rule for one list from keeping some codes secret for private use to letting anyone claim an unused code by asking first.

subtitle: Replaces vendor and private-use code points in the MPLS LSP Ping registries with First Come First Served and sets clear handling for unknown TLVs.

tldr.problem: The MPLS LSP Ping registries used Private Use and Vendor Private Use code points that could collide in production networks, too many code points were called experimental, and RFC 8029 used the words mandatory and optional in a confusing way.
tldr.mechanism: It changes Private Use to First Come First Served for the TLV and sub-TLV registries, renames Specification Required to RFC Required, carves out four Experimental Use code points, and rewrites the RFC 8029 text on unrecognized TLVs.
tldr.outcome: Registries now follow RFC 8126 terminology and vendors register code points rather than picking them privately. It updates RFC 8029 and RFC 8611 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9041 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2021 that updates RFC 8029 and RFC 8611. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why the Registries Change
sections.content:
The RFC lists several reasons. When the LSP Ping registry was created, it was assumed that code points allocated by Experimental RFCs would be experimental, but a code point in a public IANA registry is available to any type of document. The number of experimental code points was also larger than is normal for Experimental Use.

The words mandatory and optional were also used differently in RFC 8029 than elsewhere. There, a mandatory TLV means an action is required if the TLV is not recognized. Other RFCs use it for a TLV that must be present in a message.

Private Use and Vendor Private Use code points are allowed in production networks, so two vendors could use the same value with different meanings, causing hard-to-debug protocol issues. With First Come First Served (FCFS) code points this cannot happen. Vendors with existing code on such points should register them as FCFS once this document is published.
sections.eli5: If two kids secretly pick the same secret number for different games, they get mixed up. A sign-up sheet avoids that.

sections.title: Namespaces, Registries and Subregistries
sections.content:
The RFC fixes three terms. A namespace is a top-level registry, such as the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) Ping Parameters namespace. A registry holds code points and lists registration procedures, for example the TLVs registry. A subregistry holds sub-code-points scoped by a code point or set of code points, for example Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21.

It also expands abbreviations used in the Return Codes registry, including BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection), DDMAP (Downstream Detailed Mapping), FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class), OAM, PM and RSC (Return Subcode).
sections.eli5: Think of a big filing cabinet (namespace), its drawers (registries), and folders inside the drawers (subregistries).

sections.title: Message Type, Reply Mode and Return Code Registries
sections.content:
The Message Types, Reply Modes and Return Codes registries get minor changes. For range 252-255 the term Vendor Private Use becomes Private Use. In range 192-247 Specification Required becomes RFC Required and the note Experimental RFC needed is removed. Four code points, 248-251, are taken from that range for Experimental Use. Code point 0 is marked Reserved, except in Return Codes where 0 stays assigned as No Return Code.

The Private Use and Experimental Use ranges carry the note Reserved, not to be assigned.
sections.eli5: The numbers 0 to 255 are split into zones: strict, easy, test and private. This update marks a small test zone and renames the others.

sections.title: TLV and Sub-TLV Registration Ranges
sections.content:
TLVs and sub-TLVs with a type in 0-32767 require a response if not recognized. Those in 32768-65535 can be silently dropped. Each half is split into Standards Action, RFC Required, Experimental Use and First Come First Served ranges. See the table for the exact values.

The Experimental Use ranges are taken from space previously called Specification Required and RFC Required. The term Vendor Private Use in the assignment listings becomes First Come First Served. The Sub-TLVs for TLV Type 9 subregistry is not updated.
sections.eli5: Codes in the low half are "you must tell me if you do not understand". Codes in the high half are "fine to ignore". Each half has strict, easy, test and sign-up zones.

sections.title: Handling Unrecognized TLVs
sections.content:
Unrecognized TLVs and sub-TLVs in the Experimental Use and FCFS ranges are handled like any others. If one from 31740-31743 (Experimental Use) or 31744-32767 (FCFS) is unrecognized, a Return Code of 2 (One or more of the TLVs was not understood) must be sent in the echo response. If one from 64508-64511 or 64512-65535 is unrecognized, the receiver can silently drop it, step over it, or send an error message.

The IETF does not prescribe how experimental or private networks handle these TLVs. The rule applies to standards-compliant implementations.

The RFC also rewrites two paragraphs of RFC 8029 Section 3 and the start of Section 3.8, dropping the words mandatory and optional. Types below 32768 MUST either be supported or cause Return Code 2. For types of 32768 or more, an implementation SHOULD ignore and step over the TLV, and MAY send Return Code 2.
sections.eli5: If a message has a part you do not know, the low-numbered parts mean you must say so. The high-numbered ones you may skip quietly.

sections.title: IANA Changes and Updates to RFC 8611
sections.content:
IANA updated the MPLS LSP Ping Parameters namespace: Message Types, Reply Modes, Return Codes, TLVs and the Sub-TLV registries for types 1/16/21, 6, 11, 20, 23 and 27. This document was added as a reference for each.

The RFC also updates Section 13.4.1 of RFC 8611, so the Sub-TLVs for TLV Type 6 registry uses the same ranges as the other TLV registries.
sections.eli5: The librarian updated every list to the new rules and noted this document as the reason.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document updates IANA registries and clarifies terminology. It does not change how the code points are used, and so should create no new threats. The RFC argues the clarifications improve security, since consistent implementations are harder to attack.
sections.eli5: Only the labels on the lists changed, not how the machines work, so no new danger. Clearer rules help everyone behave the same way.
